# Configuration layering design

Design note for the shared configuration base layer across the three shipped adapters (MCP
server, OpenCode plugin, Pi extension). It records the parameter taxonomy, the precedence
model, and the per-adapter composition so the design survives between conversations. Host
capability facts live in [control-matrix.md](../research/control-matrix.md); the config
surface inventory was verified against the code on 2026-10-23.

## Problem

The state this design replaced — recorded here as history, not as the present. The option
pipeline was already single-sourced (names, defaults, clamping in
`src/core/constants.ts` → `src/core/env.ts` → `src/core/options.ts`), but the *channels*
that fed it were fragmented per host, and a multi-host user configured the same intent in
up to three ways:

- **Pi** — extension runs in-process; `DEEPSEEK_*` shell variables just worked.
- **Codex** — stdio children do not inherit the parent environment, and the installer's
  `env_vars` entry forwarded **only** `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`; every other knob set in the
  shell never reached the server unless the user hand-edited `config.toml` to add each
  variable name. (The entry now forwards every `DEEPSEEK_*` name — see the Codex
  consequence in [ADR-0002](../adr/0002-shared-config-base-layer.md).)
- **OpenCode** — the plugin resolved **only** `ctx.options` (opencode.json plugin
  options, camelCase); `DEEPSEEK_*` variables configured nothing there, so the same
  knob had a second, differently-named vocabulary. (The plugin now composes
  file < environment < `ctx.options` — see the per-adapter composition below.)

One intent ("20 results, block pinterest.com"), three configuration acts, two
vocabularies, one silent-failure trap. The isolation was accidental, not chosen.

## Parameter taxonomy

Isolation versus unification is decided per class, not globally:

| Class | Parameters | Policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **API behavior** — describes the user↔DeepSeek relationship, host-independent | `count`, `maxResults`, `minRerank`, `minAuthority`, `allowUnknownAuthority`, `blockedDomains`, `includeDomains`, `language`, `searchLocalization`, `maxRetries`, `retryBaseDelayMs` | Shared base; identical everywhere unless a host layer overrides |
| **Host-sensitive** — interacts with host output caps / deadlines (OpenCode 2,000 lines / 50 KiB; Pi MCP 20 KB + 60 s; Pi extension uncapped; Claude Code 25k tokens) | `searchTimeoutMs`, `fetchTimeoutMs`, `fetchMaxChars`, `maxSummaryChars` | Shared base gives the safe default; **per-host override in the host-native layer is the recommended place** to raise them |
| **Host integration** — describes the host's tool landscape, not the API | `searchEnabled`, `fetchEnabled`, `setDefaultWebsearch`, `fetchOverrideWebfetch`, `fetchRegisterTool`, `apiKeySource` | **Deliberately isolated.** Installer-written, host-native config only; the shared file rejects them |

Security-shaped knobs (`fetchAllowedDomains`, `fetchBlockedDomains`, `fetchBlockPrivateHosts`)
are classed as API behavior: they are deployment policy about the DeepSeek call itself, and a
shared base strengthens rather than weakens them (one policy instead of three drifting ones).

## The layering model

Precedence, low → high, identical semantics in every adapter:

```text
built-in defaults  <  shared config file  <  DEEPSEEK_* environment  <  host-native config
```

- **Host-native config** means: OpenCode `ctx.options` (opencode.json plugin entry), Pi's
  `deepseekWebRetrieval` settings namespace (the two switches), and — for MCP hosts — the
  per-server `env` block in the host's MCP registration (that block is *how* an environment
  variable arrives, not a fifth layer).
- Host-native layers keep outranking the base: installer-written intent (capability tiers)
  and explicit per-host overrides always win, so the blast radius of a bad shared value is
  bounded by whatever the host layer pins.
- The two vocabularies stay as they are — `DEEPSEEK_*` snake-case names for the environment,
  camelCase `PluginOptions` keys for the file and OpenCode options — both generated from the
  same single source and documented side by side.

## The shared config file

- **Path:** `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/deepseek-web-retrieval/config.json`, defaulting to
  `~/.config/deepseek-web-retrieval/config.json`. On win32 an explicit, non-empty
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` still wins; otherwise the conventional Roaming root applies —
  `%APPDATA%\deepseek-web-retrieval\config.json`, falling back to
  `<home>\AppData\Roaming\deepseek-web-retrieval\config.json` when `%APPDATA%` is
  unset. User scope, one file. A project-scope file
  is a confirmed non-goal for this iteration (open question below).
- **Format:** JSON object; keys are the camelCase `PluginOptions` vocabulary (class 1 and 2
  only). Example:

  ```json
  {
    "count": 20,
    "blockedDomains": ["pinterest.com"],
    "language": "zh",
    "searchLocalization": "203.0.113.7"
  }
  ```

- **Validation:** the file's parsed object feeds the existing `resolvePluginOptions` —
  clamps, IP validation, and domain normalization all come along for free. Unknown keys and
  class-3 (host-integration) keys are **rejected with a one-line stderr warning** and
  otherwise ignored; a missing or unparseable file contributes nothing (a warning line for
  the unparseable case), mirroring the Pi settings reader's conventions.
- **The API key is deliberately absent.** Auth keeps its existing channels
  (`DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, OpenCode's auth store, Pi's env) — a config file is liable to end up
  synced through dotfiles, and widening key storage is a security-surface decision this
  design does not make.

## Per-adapter composition

- **MCP server** (`src/mcp/serve.ts`): `resolveEnvOptions(env)` becomes
  `resolveEnvOptions(env, readFileOptions())` — file keys under environment keys. The server
  reads the file itself, so **the Codex `env_vars` trap disappears** regardless of what the
  host forwards.
- **Pi extension** (`src/pi/extension.ts`): `resolveExtensionOptions` inserts the file
  between defaults and the environment; the settings namespace stays on top, unchanged.
- **OpenCode plugin** (`src/opencode/plugin.ts`): `resolvePluginOptions(ctx.options)` becomes
  `resolvePluginOptions({ ...fileOptions(), ...pluginOptionsFromEnv(process.env), ...ctx.options })`
  — file, then environment, then the host layer. Additive only: existing opencode.json
  options keep winning exactly as before; the change is that the file and environment now
  work on this host too.

## Installer changes

- **Codex `env_vars`:** enumerate **every** `DEEPSEEK_*` name (generated from
  `src/core/constants.ts`, the single source) instead of only `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, so
  environment overrides work on Codex without hand-editing `config.toml`. The note the
  installer prints is updated to match.
- No other host artifacts change: the installer never writes the shared file (it is a user
  authoring surface, like a shell profile), and capability tiers stay where they are.

## Visibility

A bad shared value now fails everywhere at once, so effective configuration must be visible:

- The MCP server's startup stderr line (already printing the client identity and enabled
  tools) additionally prints **deviations from defaults only** — e.g.
  `config: count=20 blockedDomains=1 language=zh` — keeping the line short while showing
  every non-default knob a multi-layer resolution produced.
- The OpenCode plugin and Pi extension print the same deviation summary once, at
  registration time, through their host's logging channel (implementer picks the least
  noisy channel per host; the content contract is "non-default effective values").
- `deepseek-web-retrieval config` is the user-facing arm: it prints every knob with its
  value and source, replays the file's warnings where a human actually looks, and its
  `--search` variant verifies the whole chain (key, config, network) with one billed
  request.

## What this design does not change

- `need_content` is no longer hardcoded `false` — it became a per-call tool parameter
  with a deployment-owned envelope
  ([search-content-design.md](search-content-design.md),
  [ADR-0003](../adr/0003-need-content-per-call-boolean.md)).
- `ori_question` remains per-call-only — supplied through the tool input named
  `original_question` (with the Pi session fallback) and sent to the API as `ori_question`;
  it is not configurable.
- Auth surfaces, capability tiers, and the installer's plan/confirm flow.

## Testing

- Unit: file reader (missing / unparseable / unknown-key / class-3-key rejection with
  warning), precedence matrix per adapter (defaults < file < env < host) asserted through
  each adapter's existing resolution entry points.
- The installer's Codex plan snapshot gains the full `env_vars` list.
- Existing suites stay green; e2e scenarios unaffected (the file is absent in CI, which is
  itself the empty-layer case).

## Rollout

Additive and non-breaking: no existing configuration loses effect, no precedence between
existing layers changes. Documentation updates ship with the code: README gains a
"Configuration" section with the precedence table and the two-vocabulary table; the host
guides' option tables gain a shared-file column; the control-matrix note's Pi sentence
("There is no per-extension options channel: the runtime config surface is the
`DEEPSEEK_*` environment") is updated to name the file as part of that surface. All of
these updates are shipped and in place.

**Amendment, 2026-10-23** — two changes approved after this design was confirmed alter
the effective behavior of *untouched* configurations, superseding the "no existing
configuration loses effect" sentence for those two knobs:

1. `maxResults` now follows the effective `count` when unset, so `count`-only
   configurations return `count` results instead of silently truncating to the old
   default of 10 (the one-directional asymmetry is documented at the resolution site in
   `src/core/options.ts`).
2. Transient failures (408/425/429/5xx) retry twice by default instead of zero
   (rationale and the dated vendor-survey correction live in
   `docs/research/search-api-defaults.md`).

## Decisions (confirmed 2026-10-23)

1. **Project-scope file:** not in this iteration — hosts already own project-scope
   semantics, and the extra precedence row is not yet earned by demand.
2. **Invalid-key warnings:** one stderr line per bad key at first resolution — the noise
   buys typo detection (`"retries"` vs `"maxRetries"`) in a hand-edited file.
3. **File naming:** `config.json` inside the `~/.config/deepseek-web-retrieval/`
   directory (win32: `%APPDATA%\deepseek-web-retrieval\`) — room for future siblings.
4. **ADR:** the layering decision is recorded as
   [ADR 0002](../adr/0002-shared-config-base-layer.md) alongside this design note.

# Installer design

Design note for the install-time flow, shipped as the `deepseek-web-retrieval init`,
`uninstall`, and `list` subcommands for **OpenCode, Pi, Codex, and Claude Code**. It records how the
[control tiers](../research/control-matrix.md) map to the artifacts the installer emits, so the design
survives between conversations. Research backing lives in
[control-matrix.md](../research/control-matrix.md); host facts in [hosts.jsonc](../hosts.jsonc).
Remaining hosts get host modules here as their guides ship.
Examples involving other hosts describe design requirements for future modules;
the current CLI accepts only the four shipped hosts above.

## Principles

- **Never overwrite user configuration without the user's knowledge.** Every write is
  shown as a plan — old value → new value, per file — and confirmed before it is
  applied. Single-value keys are snapshotted so rollback can restore what was there.
- **Post-install behavior and impact scope must be controllable and knowable.** The
  installer reports what changes, which existing tools, rules, and MCP servers the
  choice affects, what stops working, and how to undo it. If a choice cannot fully take
  effect — a higher configuration layer outranks it — that is reported, never silently
  dropped.

## Goal

At install time the user makes two decisions: per capability (search and fetch
independently), how strongly the tools are routed — and separately, the effective scope
of the whole install.

- **Optional** — registered, the model picks freely.
- **Preferred** — registered plus rules steering the model toward them.
- **Forced** — deterministic routing (replacement, exclusion, or de-facto).
- **Off** — the DeepSeek capability is hidden from the model through the adapter's
  registration switch or Codex's host-side `disabled_tools` filter; the mapping below
  describes each path. Both off refuses to install anything.
- **Scope** — project-level (this checkout, shareable via VCS) or global (every project
  for that host on the machine).

## Stock configuration

The tier definitions assume a clean host. Real installs land on configuration that
already exists, and the installer uses three phases:

1. **Detect.** Read the host config, the rules files, and the registered MCP servers.
   Report the conflict surface: existing rules steering toward another web tool; other
   web-capable MCP servers already on the field; array-valued keys the plan must merge
   into rather than replace (Cline's `disabledTools`, Claude Code's `permissions.deny`,
   permissions `exclude` arrays, Codex's and Devin's `disabled_tools`); and higher
   layers (Claude Code managed policy — its
   existence is checked by the claude-code module; Devin enterprise team settings) that
   would outrank what the installer writes.
2. **Merge or snapshot.** Array keys merge with existing entries, recording exactly
   which entries the installer appended; single-value keys (`websearch.provider`, Pi's
   `exposure`) snapshot the prior value before overwriting; files the installer creates
   are tracked as created. Nothing is written until the user approves the full plan.
3. **Verify.** After applying, re-read the files and confirm the planned values and rules
   were written. Runtime tool visibility and model routing are checked by host-specific
   end-to-end scenarios, not by the installer itself.

## Tier semantics against stock configuration

- **Optional keeps built-in routing unchanged**: it registers the DeepSeek capability
  without preference rules or competitor exclusion. An existing DeepSeek registration
  may still need replacement, which the plan shows and snapshots; inspect the preview.
- **Preferred** can conflict without any config being touched: existing rules pointing
  at another web tool produce contradictory instructions whose outcome depends on each
  host's load order (Claude Code concatenates every level; Devin ranks team above
  project above user); competing MCP servers stay on the field; and approval-friction
  asymmetry (for example Cursor's `autoAcceptWebSearch` making the built-in search
  zero-friction) can outweigh prompt-level steering. The installer surfaces these
  conditions; it does not resolve them.
- **Forced is conditional**: the exclusion kill switches remove the built-in
  competitor, not third-party web MCP servers — those must be excluded too (the
  per-host keys cover them), or routing is not actually forced.
  - Per-host exclusion of detected web-capable MCP servers: Pi's per-server
    `enabled` key lets the plan disable them (each prior value snapshotted for
    uninstall); Claude Code excludes them the same way via server-level
    `mcp__<server>` deny rules appended to `permissions.deny`; Codex has no
    per-server kill switch, so a detected web-capable competitor makes the plan
    refuse the tier instead of promising non-exclusive routing; OpenCode's forced
    is replacement, which no third-party server overrides.
  - Detection classifies a server web-capable from its name plus its
    command/args/url — a heuristic the plan always discloses.
  - Blast radius: forced also overrides explicit user choices (OpenCode's
    `websearch.provider`), and its deny rules affect workflows beyond this
    project (a Claude Code deny cannot be carved out by allow rules), so the plan
    must state the blast radius before the user approves it.
- **Forced is not universally available**: where hosts.jsonc records `forced: "none"`
  (Cursor's search today), the wizard does not offer the tier — the tier-level analogue
  of the scope rule below (honor or report, never silently downgrade: never offer what
  cannot be delivered). Some kill
  switches are session-scoped (Copilot fetch's `--deny-tool`/`--excluded-tools` flags);
  an installer cannot persist them, so the plan reports that the exclusion evaporates on
  restart and offers what persistence exists.

## Scope

The effective scope is a first-class install-time choice, decided by the user alongside
the tiers — not inferred from the artifacts. The installer maps the choice onto the
host's scope pairs (Pi's agent dir versus `.pi/`,
Cursor's `cli-config.json` versus `.cursor/cli.json`, Claude Code's
settings hierarchy, OpenCode's global versus project config) under three rules:

- **Honor or report, never silently downgrade.** Some keys exist at only one scope:
  Devin's `disabled_tools` is user-level only (project config allows just
  `permissions`, `read_config_from`, and `hooks`); Cline's
  `global-settings.json` and MCP settings file are user-scope at 0.0.13. When the
  chosen scope cannot be honored for an artifact, the plan says so and offers the
  alternative — the global fallback for a kill switch, or a different tier that works
  at project scope — instead of quietly writing to the other scope.
- **Blast radius is part of the plan.** Global scope changes every project the user
  opens with that host; project scope normally writes into one checkout, while shared
  config fallbacks such as Codex's retain user-wide effects. Project-local artifacts are
  often committed, which shares the config and rules with the whole team — including the
  `${DEEPSEEK_API_KEY}` expansion that relies on each member's environment. The impact
  report states which applies.
- **Layers above the user still outrank the choice.** Managed, enterprise, and system
  layers override anything the installer writes at either scope; the detect phase
  reports them instead of failing silently.

Uninstall follows the files recorded for the chosen scope, including Codex's user-level
config even for a project-scope install; list shows those actual paths. The invariant is
guarded, not just assumed: two records for one host never claim the same file. When a
scope choice would overlap the other scope's record — Codex's project-scope fallback
onto `~/.codex/config.toml` beside a global install — the plan refuses with guidance,
and uninstall runs the same check defensively before touching anything.

Shared config files also carry an owner-only sidecar beside the actual file
(`.config.toml.deepseek-web-retrieval.codex.owner.json` for Codex). It points to the
owning install record and project directory, so two different project directories
cannot both claim the same global config, even with different `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`
values. Planning reports this metadata write; apply acquires the claim before
writing config and rechecks ownership, and uninstall releases it. A failed first
apply releases its new claim; a failed re-init retains the previous owner's claim.
Project-local configs and shared rules blocks do not need these sidecars.

For installs created before this ownership metadata existed, re-run init from the
original project and scope to establish the claim. An installer-style registration
without a record at the requested location is refused rather than adopted as a new
snapshot. If an identical registration was created manually, remove it before init.
Do not delete an ownership sidecar while its install is still active.

## Rollback

Uninstall restores overwritten values from their snapshots only while the current value
still matches what the installer wrote; later user edits are kept and reported. Merged
arrays lose only matching entries the installer appended, and managed rules blocks are
removed while surrounding user content is retained. Installer-created config files are
deleted only when left empty; an empty rules file is also removed. TOML comments are not
restored because the codec reserializes the document. The
[OpenCode v2 guide](../agents/opencode-v2.md) documents the failure mode this
avoids: `plugin remove` deletes the plugin entry but leaves `websearch.provider`
pointing at the removed plugin, and the user must clean up by hand.

## Tier-to-artifact mapping

Pi has two integration paths (`--path extension` by default, `--path mcp` as the fallback);
the artifacts below name the path where they differ.

| Choice | Artifacts |
| --- | --- |
| Optional | Host config registering the integration: Pi's extension path appends an `npm:<package>` source to `packages` in settings.json; the MCP paths register the server (Pi's MCP entry needs `"exposure": "direct"`; the extension path needs nothing — extension tools are `direct` by Pi's own default) |
| Preferred | The above plus a rules file for the host (file names per host in the [per-host reference](../research/control-matrix.md#per-host-reference)); the rules name the path's tool ids (`deepseek_web_search` for the extension, `mcp__deepseek__deepseek_web_search` for MCP) |
| Forced (replacement) | OpenCode plugin options (`setDefaultWebsearch` / `fetchOverrideWebfetch`) |
| Forced (exclusion) | The built-in competitor's kill switch (per-host keys in the per-host reference), plus exclusion of any other web-capable MCP servers the detect phase found — host by host below |
| Forced (de-facto) | Nothing beyond the Optional artifacts — no competitor exists |
| Off | A host-native removal of the capability's tool — host by host below |

Forced (exclusion), host by host:

- **Pi** sets each detected web-capable server's `enabled` key to `false`.
- **Claude Code** appends server-level `mcp__<server>` deny rules to
  `permissions.deny`, merging with the user's own entries.
- **Codex**, lacking a per-server kill switch, refuses the tier instead.
- **Pi's extension path** additionally refuses when a web-capable
  `packages`/`extensions` source is listed in settings.json (no per-package kill
  switch exists).

Off, host by host:

- **Codex** writes the capability's raw tool name into the server entry's
  `disabled_tools` (host-native: the tool leaves the model's context; the user's
  own entries in that array are kept).
- **Claude Code** appends the capability's full tool id (`mcp__deepseek__*`) to
  `permissions.deny` — the same host-native removal.
- **The remaining MCP entry** (Pi's fallback) writes the capability's false-only
  server-side switch instead (`DEEPSEEK_ENABLE_SEARCH` / `DEEPSEEK_ENABLE_FETCH`).
- **Pi's extension path** writes the same switches into the
  `deepseekWebRetrieval` settings namespace the extension reads at load.

Both capabilities off refuses to install.

OpenCode additionally appends `permissions` allow entries for exactly the tools it
registers (`websearch`, `deepseek_fetch`, and `webfetch` when fetch is forced), merged
into any existing `permissions` array rather than replacing it.

## Non-negotiables

- **Cost warning on the Forced tier.** Search and Fetch are billed per successful
  request; deterministic routing removes both the model's discretion and its restraint as
  a cost brake. Every forced-tier plan carries a note naming the README's "Privacy and
  cost" section.
- **Rules content.** Name the full tool ids the host will see (`mcp__deepseek__deepseek_web_search`
  over MCP, `deepseek_web_search` over Pi's extension), state trigger conditions rather than
  unconditional preference, and list exclusions (localhost/private-network URLs go to local
  fetch tools; the server blocks them by default). Emit routing guidance only for the
  capability selected as preferred; an optional capability stays optional even when the
  other capability is preferred. Missing, reversed, or duplicate block markers refuse
  planning, apply, and uninstall without deleting the ambiguous surrounding text.

## Implementation notes

- JSON edits go through `jsonc-parser` (the library behind VS Code's JSON support), so
  comments and formatting in `opencode.jsonc` and Pi's `mcp.json` survive apply and
  uninstall; TOML edits go through `smol-toml` and drop comments, which the plan reports
  as a note. The hand-written JSONC stripper that predated this lived in `scripts/jsonc.ts`.
- Install records live per host and scope (global under
  `~/.config/deepseek-web-retrieval/`, project under `.deepseek-web-retrieval/`); they
  record snapshots, appended entries, created files, and created path prefixes — never
  full file contents, so other servers' secrets stay out of the install record.
- Re-applying over a previous init inherits the original snapshots instead of recording
  the installer's own output as the "previous" value. Pi forced re-inits keep their
  competitor-disable ops even when those servers are already disabled, so orphan
  reverts cannot re-enable a still-excluded competitor.
- Verify is file-level: after apply it re-reads each written file and asserts every op
  holds (set values in place, appended entries present, rules block present). Higher
  layers are a plan-time detect concern; Claude Code documents one (managed policy), and
  the claude-code module reports an existing managed-settings.json instead of failing
  silently. The other shipped hosts document no layer above user config.
- Only a bare `--apply` enables writes; assigning a value such as `--apply=false`
  is a usage error and writes nothing.
- `--pin` is opt-in version pinning: the ref written into host config gets the
  running CLI's version appended (`name` becomes `name@<version>`; a ref already
  ending in a version keeps it), so a host resolves that exact release instead of
  the latest publish. Without the flag the ref stays unpinned, byte-identical to
  before; re-running `init --pin` from a newer CLI moves the pin. Ref identity —
  orphan, upgrade, and unexcludable-competitor detection — compares package names
  with the `@version` suffix stripped (`samePackageName` in ownership.ts), so a
  pinned ref still matches the lineage an earlier init registered.
- File verification precedes the install-record commit. A write or verification
  failure restores the pre-apply files and record and checks the restored values.
  `ApplyError.status` is `rolled_back` only after recovery and new-claim cleanup
  succeed. Otherwise it is `recovery_required`, with the original cause and a
  recovery report; new claims remain while file or record recovery is incomplete.
  Obsolete claims are released after commit. If that cleanup fails, the verified
  install and new record are retained and reported explicitly for recovery.

## Server-side gap (resolved)

The MCP server now honors `DEEPSEEK_ENABLE_SEARCH` / `DEEPSEEK_ENABLE_FETCH`
(false-only switches through the shared option pipeline) and refuses to start when both
are disabled; the OpenCode plugin honors the matching `searchEnabled` / `fetchEnabled`
options. Per-capability control is uniform across hosts, including those without
host-side tool filtering.

## Hosts without an installer story

Cursor, Devin, GitHub Copilot, and Cline still have no
host module; their artifacts (from the tier-to-artifact mapping) remain hand-edited
config until a module lands here. OpenCode's `opencode plugin add` remains available but
cannot pass options or manage snapshots; `init` supersedes it for tiered installs.

## Persistence and concurrent operations

Install records distinguish absent files from invalid or unreadable files. The
reader validates version, host/scope identity, tiers, file metadata, and recorded
operations before an install or uninstall can use undo state. `list` reports a
bad record instead of silently omitting it. Restore the record from backup or
repair access before retrying; deleting it can discard the original snapshots.

Config and record writes use private temporary files in the target directory,
verify the temporary contents, flush the file, then rename and flush the directory
(on POSIX). Existing config permissions and valid symbolic links are preserved;
records are always mode 0600. A failed write before rename leaves the old file
intact. This makes each file replacement atomic, not the entire multi-file install.
The apply rollback remains responsible for caught errors; power-loss recovery is
not an automatic transaction replay.

Apply and uninstall acquire a record operation lock before reading undo state,
then locks for every config/rules path they may mutate, including orphan reverts.
Locks follow canonical paths, so another project or symlink alias cannot bypass a
shared-file lock. A plan whose prior record changed is refused, even if its only
edits append arrays. Preview generation is read-only and does not reserve locks.

Operation locks are directories ending in `.deepseek-web-retrieval.lock`, with
owner PID and start time inside. Ordinary success or failure releases them. A
killed process may leave a lock; to recover from one:

1. Confirm no installer is currently running.
2. Inspect the config, install record, and persistent ownership claims.
3. Restore any inconsistent state.
4. Remove the reported lock directory and generate a new plan.

Locks are
never stolen based only on age or PID. Persistent `.owner.json` claims remain a
separate safeguard against two installations owning one shared config.

# Search content design

Design note for `need_content` — DeepSeek's inline-content search flag — across the two
model-facing adapters (the MCP server and the Pi extension). It records the parameter
split (who decides what), the envelope arithmetic that sets the defaults, the rendering
contract, and the per-adapter composition, so the design survives between conversations.
The facts it builds on are in [search-inline-content.md](../research/search-inline-content.md)
(baseline 2026-10-23); the decision record is
[ADR-0003](../adr/0003-need-content-per-call-boolean.md). This note was verified against
the code on 2026-10-24.

## Problem

The wire parameter is a boolean the repo hardcoded `false`: search results carried a
summary digest (`summary` falling back to `snippet`) and never a page body. An agent
needing bodies had to guess which URLs to fetch from the digests — a wrong guess is a
silent miss. Turning the flag on naively is not safe either: DeepSeek documents **no**
size bound for the returned `content`, host output caps run as tight as Pi's 20 KB
MCP-path truncation (middle truncation — whole results vanish), and the 30 s default
search timeout does not budget for the server-side page crawl the flag triggers.

## The parameter split

Two axes, two owners:

- **The agent owns the boolean.** `need_content` is a per-call, optional tool parameter
  on every surface where this package defines the search tool's inputs (the MCP server
  and the Pi extension), defaulting to `false`. It rides `SearchRequest.needContent`
  (the `oriQuestion` pattern), not the resolved options — it changes nothing in option
  state, only what that one call sends. Task type is the biggest determinant of whether
  content helps, and only the model knows the task; the repo's other per-call parameters
  (`count`, fetch `maxChars`) are the precedent: always exposed, never mode-gated.
- **The deployment owns the envelope.** Two deployment-level knobs — never tool
  parameters — apply whenever content flows: `searchContentMaxChars` (per-result body
  budget) and `searchContentTimeoutMs` (the timeout a content call runs on, replacing
  `searchTimeoutMs` for that call; the per-call `timeoutMs` cap still wins if shorter).
  The model cannot see which host caps its output, so it cannot own a budget.

## The envelope

Defaults from the host-cap arithmetic in the research note:

- `searchContentMaxChars` defaults to **1,500**. At the default `count=10`, bodies plus
  the ~1k chars of per-result metadata land near 16 KB — under the tightest published
  cap (Pi's 20 KB MCP-path truncation) for Latin-script pages. CJK-heavy responses
  measure 3 bytes per character toward that cap, so a CJK-focused deployment on a
  20 KB host should lower the budget or the count (at 1,500 chars/result, count ≈ 13 is
  the 20 KB ceiling even for Latin text). The native Pi extension bypasses the MCP
  layer entirely — neither its 20 KB truncation nor its 60 s timeout applies — so that
  deployment can afford a larger budget.
- `searchContentTimeoutMs` defaults to **60,000** — between the 30 s search default the
  digest path keeps and the 300 s ceiling Codex allows, because the API must fetch
  every result page server-side before responding and documents no latency statement.

The total a response can carry is budget × count plus metadata. That product is the
deployment's arithmetic to run when tuning either knob; the core does not narrow any
parameter's range at runtime (see Decisions).

## Per-adapter composition

- **MCP server**: `need_content` in the zod input schema, forwarded as
  `needContent: need_content === true`.
- **Pi extension**: the same parameter in the TypeBox schema (`SEARCH_PARAMETERS` stays
  a module-level constant on both surfaces — the schema is unconditional), forwarded the
  same way.
- **OpenCode**: no change. The host fixes the `websearch` provider input to `query`
  (the upstream gap that already blocks per-call `count`), so the provider stays
  summary-only; the envelope knobs resolve through the shared pipeline and are dormant
  there. Documented next to the count gap in
  [opencode-v2.md](../agents/opencode-v2.md).
- **Installer**: no artifacts change. The knob defaults are global and the deviation
  lines on every adapter already report non-default values through the config
  vocabulary.

## Processing and rendering

`processResults` is mode-agnostic: a present, non-empty `content` **replaces** the
digest (the summary is a proxy for the body it compresses), clamped to
`searchContentMaxChars` with an ellipsis marker when shortened; an empty, whitespace,
or missing body — the API documents per-result absence, and `need_content: false`
responses carry an empty string — falls back to the digest path. `searchContentMaxChars:
0` treats the body as absent. Each result carries `contentKind: "page" | "digest"` so
the renderer knows the source: page bodies render as Markdown indented into the list
item (heading and list structure survive); digests stay compacted to one line, as
summaries always were. The `structuredContent` mirror carries the same `content`
string on hosts that read it.

## What this design does not change

- Billing behavior: Search bills per successful request; `need_content` is not a price
  modifier, so a content call costs the same as a digest call (and can replace fetch
  calls at the same per-request price).
- The fetch tool, its `maxChars` parameter, and the two-tool architecture — a content
  call replaces *some* fetches, not the deep-read path.
- `maxSummaryChars`, thresholds, dedup, query composition, and degradation.
- `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` (5 MiB) — still the outer guard, still erroring rather than
  truncating; the per-result budget keeps responses far below it.

## Testing

Wire assertions on both model-facing adapters (`need_content: true` reaching the wire;
`false` by default), client tests for the flag and the timeout selection
(`contentTimeoutMs` used only when the call asks for content), `processResults` tests
for the body-over-digest precedence, the budget clamp and marker, the empty-body
fallback, and the zero-budget drop, and format tests for the two rendering shapes.

## Rollout

Shipped behind default-`false` behavior: with no configuration and no parameter use,
every surface behaves exactly as before (the wire still says `need_content: false`).
Deployments opt in per call by the model, per host by the two envelope knobs. No
installer or shared-file migration; the knobs join the config vocabulary and the
generated knob table.

## Decisions (confirmed 2026-10-24)

1. The boolean is a per-call tool parameter, always exposed on the MCP server and the
   Pi extension; no config mode gates it.
2. The envelope is deployment-only: `searchContentMaxChars` (1,500) and
   `searchContentTimeoutMs` (60,000), never tool parameters.
3. A page body replaces the digest; empty bodies fall back to it.
4. `need_content` does not control other parameters — neither their availability nor
   their value ranges. Effects may be conditional (the envelope knobs apply only when
   content flows); domains are static. No surveyed vendor couples a content flag to
   another parameter's range ([search-inline-content.md](../research/search-inline-content.md)),
   and a silent runtime narrowing (say, of `count`) would be a decision the model
   cannot see. The budget × count arithmetic is the deployment's to run.
5. OpenCode stays summary-only until the upstream provider input widens.
6. The descriptions state facts — mechanics, latency, price, magnitude, the fetch
   alternative — and no usage policy. When content is worth it is the model's per-call
   judgment (or a user's rules file per deployment), not the tool author's; if usage
   data later shows the parameter systematically ignored or overused, that is the point
   to add minimal steering, decided by evidence.

  (`exposure: "codemode"`); `"exposure": "direct"` declares them like built-ins — the
  prerequisite for every tier. SSE is rejected. Text results over 20 KB are
  middle-truncated with the full text saved to a file, and the per-request default
  timeout is 60 s. Pi is content-first for the model, with a `structuredContent`

  `outputSchema`.

- **AGENTS.md is the de-facto rules standard.** Seven of the eight hosts read it

# MCP compatibility across hosts

This note answers one question for the shipped MCP server: do the hosts in the
[support matrix](../integration.md) speak the same MCP protocol standard? Short answer: they all
speak MCP, but not the same revision. MCP has split into two eras, hosts negotiate different
revisions, and one dual-era server covers them all.

The seven MCP-capable hosts in the matrix span **four different negotiated revisions**:
`2024-11-05` (Cline), `2025-06-18` (Codex), `2025-11-25` (Pi), and
`2026-07-28` (Claude Code, Devin, GitHub Copilot) — plus Cursor, whose revision no primary
source pins. OpenCode is out of scope here: its shipped integration is the
[native plugin adapter](../agents/opencode-v2.md), not MCP.

**Research baseline:** 2026-10-19, using the same version locks as the host support matrix in
[integration.md](../integration.md). Claims are cited to primary sources: the MCP specification,
official host docs and changelogs, npm registry manifests, and host source code at the locked
versions.

## Protocol revisions

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open specification, originally from Anthropic, now
developed in the open at [modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). The
protocol version is a date string, not semver; a revision is published only for breaking
changes.

| Revision | Date | Key changes | Transports |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `2024-11-05` | 2024-11-05 | Initial revision ("MCP 1.0"): `initialize` handshake, capabilities, tools/resources/prompts, sampling, roots, logging. | stdio, HTTP+SSE |
| `2025-03-26` | 2025-03-26 | OAuth 2.1 authorization; **Streamable HTTP replaces HTTP+SSE** (deprecated, not removed); JSON-RPC batching; tool annotations. | stdio, Streamable HTTP, HTTP+SSE (deprecated) |
| `2025-06-18` | 2025-06-18 | Structured tool output (`structuredContent`, `outputSchema`); servers are OAuth 2.1 resource servers (RFC 9728/8707); elicitation; `MCP-Protocol-Version` header required on HTTP; batching removed. | stdio, Streamable HTTP |
| `2025-11-25` | 2025-11-25 | OIDC discovery for auth servers; icons; elicitation rework; experimental tasks; JSON Schema 2020-12. | stdio, Streamable HTTP |
| `2026-07-28` (current) | 2026-07-28 | **Stateless core**: no `initialize` handshake, no sessions/`Mcp-Session-Id`; version and capabilities carried per-request in `_meta`; new mandatory `server/discover`; server-initiated requests (sampling/elicitation/roots) replaced by Multi Round-Trip Requests; Roots/Sampling/Logging and HTTP+SSE deprecated. | stdio, Streamable HTTP |

Sources: per-revision changelogs ([2025-03-26](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/changelog),
[2025-06-18](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/changelog),
[2025-11-25](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/changelog),
[2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog)) and the
[current version pointer](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning).

### Two eras

The spec now distinguishes
[Legacy (`2025-11-25` and earlier) and Modern (`2026-07-28`+)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning)
versions:

- **Legacy** clients open with an `initialize` handshake and negotiate one version:
  ["If the server supports the requested protocol version, it MUST respond with the same
  version. Otherwise, the server MUST respond with another protocol version it
  supports."](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/lifecycle)
- **Modern** clients send no handshake; every request declares its version in `_meta` (and in
  the `MCP-Protocol-Version` HTTP header). An unsupported version gets
  `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError` with a `supported` list, and the client retries.
- A server MAY implement both behaviors; a dual-era server picks per connection from how the
  client opens. The published
  [compatibility matrix](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/versioning#compatibility-matrix)
  is the crux: **a legacy client fails against a modern-only server** (no fall-forward), while
  a modern client falls back to the legacy handshake (and, if needed, to deprecated HTTP+SSE).

### Official SDK support

Two release lines of the official TypeScript SDK ([docs](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/blob/main/docs/protocol-versions.md)):

- **v1.x** — [`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk)
  (latest 1.32.1). Implements the spec up to `2025-11-25` and
  [will not gain `2026-07-28` support](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk);
  receives fixes for at least six months after v2 shipped (2026-07-27). A v1 server echoes any
  client-requested version in its supported list
  (`2024-11-05` … `2025-11-25`, [source](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/blob/v1.x/src/server/index.ts)),
  so it auto-compatibles with older clients.
- **v2** — [`@modelcontextprotocol/server`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server)
  and `@modelcontextprotocol/client` (latest 2.3.1). Implements `2026-07-28`; `createMcpHandler`
  / `serveStdio` **serve both eras from one entry point by default**
  ([migration doc](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/blob/main/docs/migration/support-2026-07-28.md)).

## One server for all hosts

Yes — one MCP server implementation can serve every host in the matrix. The hosts do not
share one revision, but the protocol's negotiation rules and the official SDKs absorb the
differences:

1. **Tools only, text-first results.** Expose the retrieval as two tools via the `tools`
   capability; do not rely on resources, prompts, sampling, elicitation, or roots — the
   hosts' client capabilities are inconsistent (Codex has elicitation only; Pi serves
   roots). Always return readable
   text in `content` blocks, and mirror the same data in `structuredContent` — the
   spec's own backwards-compat SHOULD — except for clients that would replace the text
   with its serialized JSON: Codex *replaces* content with `structuredContent` when
   present, so the shipped server detects its `codex-mcp-client` identity (the
   initialize `clientInfo` on handshake-era connections, the per-request envelope on
   `2026-07-28`) and omits the mirror for it. Cline reads
   text content only; Pi is
   content-first, falling back to `structuredContent` only when a result has no content
   blocks (verified in `tools.ts` at v1.3.0). No `outputSchema` is declared: the SDK
   rejects text-only results for a tool with a declared schema, and no host in the
   matrix validates the schema anyway. The per-host model-channel facts behind this —
   which of `content`/`structuredContent` provably reaches the model on each host,
   native adapter paths included — are recorded in
   [result-quality-passthrough.md](result-quality-passthrough.md).
2. **stdio is the universal transport.** Every host in the matrix launches stdio servers
   with the same conceptual JSON (`mcpServers` → `command`/`args`/`env`), differing only in
   file location and cosmetic field names. stdio needs no OAuth and no URL config, and the
   spec says clients SHOULD support it whenever possible. Legacy SSE is never required —
   Codex and Pi reject it anyway.
3. **Build on the official SDK v2 dual-era serving.** One build then serves the full range:
   the `2024-11-05` floor set by Cline (v2 legacy support spans `2024-10-07`–`2025-11-25`;
   `2024-10-07` is the pre-1.0 draft version string the SDK accepts for legacy
   compatibility — it predates the spec's initial `2024-11-05` revision)
   up to the `2026-07-28` negotiators (Claude Code 2.1.274+, Devin 3000.11.92, Copilot CLI
   1.0.81+). A v1.x-built server still works today — modern clients fall back to the legacy
   handshake — but it can never offer the stateless era; v2 serves both from one entry
   point.
4. **Streamable HTTP only for a hosted deployment.** All seven MCP hosts surveyed here support it (with
   different `type` strings: `http`, `streamable-http`, `streamableHttp`), and OAuth 2.1
   resource-server behavior (RFC 9728 metadata) then applies; prefer pre-registered clients
   over the now-deprecated Dynamic Client Registration.
5. **Host quirks to design around.** Tool naming (`deepseek_web_search`,
   `deepseek_fetch`) already reflects the quirk catalog in the
   [per-host reference](control-matrix.md#per-host-reference) — name collisions and
   truncation, environment passing, output caps, and per-host approval surfaces; consult
   it per host rather than this summary.

These protocol findings describe compatibility at the research baseline, not completed
end-to-end support for every host. The shipped server exposes stdio; supported setup
guides and installer coverage are listed in the [integration model](../integration.md).

# Sourcing `ori_question` across hosts

This note answers one question: through what channel could each host in the
[support matrix](../integration.md) supply a value for the DeepSeek Search API's optional
`ori_question` request parameter — "触发搜索的用户原始问题,1~128 个字符,有助于更好地理解搜索意图" (the
user's original question that triggered the search;
[API guide](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/search), parameter table reproduced in
[search-api-defaults.md](search-api-defaults.md))? Two candidate channels are examined per host:
**(A)** a model-filled optional tool input parameter (e.g. an optional `original_question` string in
the tool's input schema), and **(B)** the adapter itself reading the surrounding session/task
context at tool-call time. At the research baseline the repo never sent the parameter; it is
now sent on the MCP path (channel A) and the Pi path (A plus B as a blank-input fallback),
while OpenCode's websearch provider path has no channel at 2.0.32 (below).

**Research baseline:** 2026-10-23, using the same version locks as
[hosts.jsonc](../hosts.jsonc) (baseline 2026-10-19): Cline 0.0.13, Codex 0.163.0
(rust-v0.163.0, rmcp 3.5.1), OpenCode 2.0.32, Pi 1.3.0, Claude Code 2.1.303, Cursor 2026.10.08,
Devin 3000.11.92, GitHub Copilot 1.0.98. Claims are cited to primary sources only: the MCP
specification, host source code at exact git tags, npm tarballs at the locked versions, and
official docs/changelogs. Where no primary source pins a fact, that is stated rather than guessed.
Protocol-revision facts per host are inherited from
[mcp-compatibility.md](mcp-compatibility.md) and not re-derived.

## What the protocol offers

MCP never carries conversation context to a server. The facts, per revision:

- **`tools/call` params are `name` + `arguments` (+ `_meta`).** The 2025-06-18 schema defines the
  params as `name` (required, string) and `arguments` (optional, free-form object with
  `additionalProperties: {}`) — the concrete `CallToolRequest` does not even enumerate `_meta`
  ([schema.json](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/main/schema/2025-06-18/schema.json));
  the same shape holds in 2024-11-05 and 2025-11-25
  ([tools pages](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools)). 2025-11-25
  adds an optional `task` field (task augmentation) and 2026-07-28 adds `inputResponses` /
  `requestState` for multi round-trip retries plus required per-request `_meta` protocol fields
  ([2026-07-28 tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools),
  [_meta](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#meta)) — none of
  these carry user or conversation data.
- **The spec assigns input validation to servers, not clients.** "Servers **MUST**: Validate all
  tool inputs"; the client-side SHOULDs cover validating *results* and showing inputs to the user —
  no revision obliges (or forbids) a client to validate model arguments against `inputSchema`
  ([security considerations](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools),
  all revisions). `inputSchema` is "JSON Schema defining expected parameters", defaulting to the
  2020-12 dialect from 2025-11-25 on. This makes an optional declared property the spec-sanctioned
  way for a model to convey extra intent.
- **"MCP has no protocol-level session."** The 2026-07-28 spec says it directly: "a server cannot
  rely on implicit per-connection state to relate one tool call to the next"
  ([Stateful Tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools#stateful-tools)),
  and the statelessness rules forbid inferring context from prior requests
  ([Statelessness](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#statelessness)).
- **Sampling cannot be abused to obtain the context.** `sampling/createMessage` is
  server-initiated with server-authored `messages`; `includeContext: "thisServer"/"allServers"`
  (soft-deprecated) includes *MCP-server* context, not the host conversation, and requests are
  human-reviewed
  ([sampling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/client/sampling)). A server
  could only ask a model to *guess* intent — not obtain the user's question.
- **Elicitation is interactive, not derivation.** `elicitation/create` asks the user a form/choice
  question and waits ([2025-06-18+](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/client/elicitation));
  it requires client capability (only Codex in this matrix has it, per
  [mcp-compatibility.md](mcp-compatibility.md)) and an explicit round trip.
- **Tasks are state machines, not context.** The experimental 2025-11-25 `Task` object is
  `taskId`/`status`/timestamps/`ttl`/`pollInterval` — no user data
  ([tasks](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/utilities/tasks)).
- **`_meta` has no context convention.** Reserved keys are enumerated; vendors may add prefixed
  keys, but no host documents sending conversation context there
  ([_meta](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/index#meta)). Codex is the
  one host observed adding its own key — `openai/entitlementContext`, carrying entitlement status
  for zero-argument read-only plugin tools
  ([trusted_access.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/codex-mcp/src/trusted_access.rs))
  — not user context.

Conclusion: **for an MCP-connected host, channel A (the tool's input schema) is the only spec-borne
channel; channel B does not exist at the protocol layer.** Whether A works in practice depends on
each host's client, below.

## Open-source hosts, from source at the lock

### Codex 0.163.0 (rust-v0.163.0)

- **No client-side argument validation.** The model's `arguments` string is parsed as JSON (empty
  allowed; invalid JSON becomes an error result) and the resulting `serde_json::Value` flows
  unchanged to rmcp's `call_tool`
  ([mcp_tool_call.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/core/src/mcp_tool_call.rs),
  [connection_manager.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/codex-mcp/src/connection_manager.rs)).
  No JSON-Schema validator exists in the tree (only `schemars`, used to *generate* schemas for
  built-in tools; codex-rs/Cargo.toml at the tag).
- **Input schemas reach the model essentially verbatim.** `mcp_tool_to_responses_api_tool` forwards
  the server's `inputSchema` as the tool's `parameters`
  ([responses_api.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tools/src/responses_api.rs));
  the only transformations are inserting an empty `properties` object when missing, sanitizing
  boolean schemas, and a default 5,000-byte budget: over-budget schemas are progressively
  compacted (strip descriptions → drop definitions → collapse deep objects → prune compositions)
  ([mcp_tool.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tools/src/mcp_tool.rs),
  [json_schema.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tools/src/json_schema.rs),
  [compaction.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tools/src/json_schema/compaction.rs)).
  A small schema with one optional string property stays intact.
- **Channel B: none.** Codex's third-party integration surface at this tag is MCP servers; there is
  no session/context API a server can call.

Verdict: **A feasible (nothing validates or strips arguments; schema forwarded), B impossible.**

### Pi 1.3.0 (v1.3.0)

- **The agent loop validates arguments against the tool's parameter schema before `execute`.**
  `validateToolArguments` clones the arguments, normalizes `null` for optional properties, coerces
  types (`Value.Convert`, plus JSON-Schema coercion for plain JSON-Schema tools), then runs a
  TypeBox `Check`; failures come back to the model as `Validation failed for tool …` error results
  ([validation.ts](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/ai/src/utils/validation.ts),
  [agent-loop.ts](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts)).
  A *declared optional* property therefore passes and reaches the tool; undeclared fields pass only
  when the schema itself permits them.
- **MCP tools: schema forwarded, params passed through.** The adapter spreads the server's
  `inputSchema` into the model-facing parameters (adding only `type: "object"` and an empty
  `properties` when missing) and passes the validated `params` to the client's `callTool`, which
  sends `{ name, arguments }` verbatim (a `_meta.progressToken` is added only when progress
  reporting is on)
  ([tools.ts](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/coding-agent/src/extensions/mcp/tools.ts),
  [client.ts](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/mcp/src/client.ts)).
- **Extension tools receive session access as a fifth `execute` argument.** At v1.3.0 the signature
  is `execute(toolCallId, params, signal, onUpdate, ctx: ExtensionToolContext)`
  ([types.ts](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/types.ts)).
  `ExtensionToolContext` extends `ExtensionContext`, whose `sessionManager` is a
  `ReadonlySessionManager` exposing `buildSessionProjection()` — returning the model-visible
  `messages: AgentMessage[]` (user messages included), plus `getEntries`/`getTree`/`getBranch`
  ([session-manager.ts](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts)).
  The extension docs at the tag document `ctx` for tools (`ctx.executeTool`, `ctx.sessionManager`)
  ([extensions.md](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.3.0/packages/coding-agent/docs/extensions.md)).
  The `ExtensionAPI` event surface (`input`, `message_end`, `tool_execution_*`) additionally lets an
  extension track the user prompt as it arrives.

Verdict: **A feasible on both paths (declared optional TypeBox property; validated, then passed
through). B feasible on the extension path via the fifth `execute` argument — the handler can read
the session's user messages at call time. B impossible via MCP** (separate process, no session
API).

### OpenCode 2.0.32

Repo provenance first: `@opencode/cli@2.0.32`'s manifest points at
[github.com/anomalyco/opencode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode), which has the `v2.0.32`
tag (commit `843a6c5`); the `opencode-ai/opencode` repository's tags stop at `v0.0.x` and hold no
2.x tag. Facts below are from the tag plus the npm tarballs at 2.0.32
(`@opencode/plugin`, `@opencode/schema`, `@opencode/client`).

- **The tool runtime validates arguments against the tool's declared input schema before
  `execute`.** `Tool.runtime.execute` decodes the model's input first: raw JSON-Schema inputs are
  converted to an Effect codec and validated; failures return `Invalid arguments for tool "…":
  … Update the arguments and call the tool again.`
  ([runtime.ts](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.0.32/packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts)).
  A plugin tool's plain JSON Schema `input` is forwarded to the model **as-is** (`inputJsonSchema`
  returns it unchanged), so a declared optional parameter is both model-visible and validated.
- **`ToolContext` carries IDs only**: `sessionID`, `agent`, `messageID`, call `id`, `signal`,
  `progress` ([tool.d.ts in @opencode/schema 2.0.32](https://registry.npmjs.org/@opencode/schema/2.0.32);
  [tool.d.ts in @opencode/plugin 2.0.32](https://registry.npmjs.org/@opencode/plugin/2.0.32)).
- **But the plugin `Context.session` domain can read the conversation.** The picked `SessionDomain`
  includes `context({ sessionID }) → SessionMessageInfo[]`, and `SessionMessageUser` has
  `text: string` — the user's prompt text — plus attachments
  ([session.d.ts](https://registry.npmjs.org/@opencode/plugin/2.0.32),
  [client types](https://registry.npmjs.org/@opencode/client/2.0.32)). Session hooks round it out:
  `"prompt"` fires with the prompt itself, `"generate"`/`"context"` with `messages: Array<Message>`
  ([session.d.ts at 2.0.32](https://registry.npmjs.org/@opencode/plugin/2.0.32)). So a tool's
  `execute` can call `ctx.session.context({ sessionID: context.sessionID })` at call time.
- **The native websearch provider interface carries only the query.**
  `WebSearch.ProviderInput = Pick<Input, "query">`, the provider context is `{ signal }`, and core
  invokes providers as `.execute({ query: input.query })`
  ([websearch.ts](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.0.32/packages/core/src/websearch.ts),
  [websearch.d.ts](https://registry.npmjs.org/@opencode/schema/2.0.32)). The model-facing
  `websearch` tool's input schema is fixed in host source to `query` alone
  ([tool/plugin/websearch.ts](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.0.32/packages/core/src/tool/plugin/websearch.ts)).
  A provider gets no sessionID, so session auto-derivation on this path is not directly possible —
  only heuristic correlation via the session hooks (which fire per model request with the
  sessionID, but no API contract binds a provider call to a session).

  Post-baseline drift check (2026-10-24): the interface is unchanged at 2.1.4, the latest npm
  release on that date (unpkg dist of `@opencode/schema`/`@opencode/plugin` 2.1.4:
  `ProviderInput = Pick<Input, "query">`, provider context `{ signal }`). Upstream requests
  filed the same day to widen this surface:
  [anomalyco/opencode#58635](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/58635) (session
  linkage in the provider execute context) and
  [#58636](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/58636) (optional per-call `count`
  passthrough) — re-check both when the baseline or the OpenCode lock bumps.

Verdict: **tool path (`deepseek_fetch` / the `webfetch` override): A feasible (validated against
the declared schema; raw JSON Schema forwarded verbatim) and B feasible
(`ctx.session.context`). Websearch provider path (the search replacement this repo ships): neither
— the input schema is host-fixed to `query`, and the provider context has no session handle.**

## What this means for this repo

- **MCP server (`src/mcp/server.ts`).** The tool `inputSchema` is the only channel any MCP host
  offers. The server declares its inputs as zod objects (`z.object({ query, original_question })`,
  `z.object({ url })`) through SDK v2's `registerTool`; zod's default behavior strips undeclared
  keys server-side, so a host-side pre-filled undeclared field would be dropped — whatever a host
  sends must be *declared* in the schema to arrive in the handler. The declared optional string
  surfaces in the JSON Schema every host in this note forwards (Codex and Pi verbatim-small,
  OpenCode verbatim, Claude Code and Copilot per changelog evidence; Cline, Cursor, Devin
  unproven but spec-conformant) — exactly the channel the shipped `original_question` rides.
- **OpenCode plugin (`src/opencode/plugin.ts`).** The fetch tools' `execute` receives a
  `ToolContext` with `sessionID`, and the plugin `Context` can read
  `ctx.session.context({ sessionID })` — user messages with their `text` — at call time, so
  channel B exists here without touching schemas. The `websearch` provider replacement — the path
  this repo uses for search — has neither channel at 2.0.32: its model-facing input schema is
  fixed in host source to `query`, and its provider context is `{ signal }` only (upstream
  requests: [#58635](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/58635),
  [#58636](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/58636)). Note also that
  `FETCH_INPUT` sets `additionalProperties: false`, which matters if a parameter is ever added on
  channel A: an undeclared field would be rejected by OpenCode's runtime validation with a
  retryable error.
- **Pi extension (`src/pi/extension.ts`).** The search handler reads the fifth `execute`
  argument (`ExtensionToolContext`), whose `sessionManager.buildSessionProjection()` returns the
  model-visible messages, user prompts included — readable synchronously at call time, so channel
  B exists on this path; the shipped adapter uses it as the blank-input fallback. Channel A is
  equally open: the TypeBox `parameters` are what the agent loop validates against, and
  `Type.Optional(Type.String(...))` properties pass validation when the model fills them. The
  extension runs in-process, so B does not pay the MCP detour.

# Passing result quality fields to the model

This note answers one question: through which channel can DeepSeek's per-result quality fields —
`rerank_score` (0–3, "≥1.5 优质"), `authority` (0–4, -1 unknown, "≥3 极权威"), `site_name`
(string|null) — reach the **model** (not the human UI) on each host at its locked version? The
repo filters on the first two in `src/core/search.ts` (thresholds default to off); at the
research baseline it dropped all three before returning — the adapters now pass them through
as a text marker plus a structured mirror (the text marker of *What this means for this
repo*, item 1, is implemented as `formatQualityMarker`).
Related: [ori-question-sourcing.md](ori-question-sourcing.md) (input side),
[search-inline-content.md](search-inline-content.md) (content volume).

**Research baseline:** 2026-10-23, using the same version locks as
[hosts.jsonc](../hosts.jsonc) (Cline 0.0.13, Codex 0.163.0, OpenCode 2.0.32, Pi 1.3.0,
Claude Code 2.1.303, Cursor 2026.10.08, Devin 3000.11.92, GitHub Copilot 1.0.98). Claims are
cited to primary sources: the MCP specification, the official TypeScript SDK as installed in
this repo (`@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.1 — the shipped artifact), host source at the
exact tags or as installed in `node_modules` (the published npm packages are themselves primary
sources), and official docs/changelogs. Prior findings in
[mcp-compatibility.md](mcp-compatibility.md) and [control-matrix.md](control-matrix.md) are
cited rather than re-derived; this note re-verified the load-bearing ones and extends them.

## What the specification says

MCP [`2025-06-18` tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools)
introduced structured output:

- Unstructured content rides in `content` (text/image/audio/resource blocks); structured
  content is "a JSON object in the `structuredContent` field."
- Backwards compatibility is a server-side SHOULD, verbatim: *"For backwards compatibility, a
  tool that returns structured content **SHOULD** also return the serialized JSON in a
  TextContent block."*
- With a declared `outputSchema`: *"Servers **MUST** provide structured results that conform to
  this schema. Clients **SHOULD** validate structured results against this schema."*
- Content blocks carry optional `annotations.audience` (`"user"` / `"assistant"`) — a spec-level
  way to mark a block as model-visible or human-visible. No host in the matrix is documented to
  honor it; treated as unpinned below.

The `2024-11-05` revision (Cline's floor) has neither `structuredContent` nor `outputSchema`.

## What the official TypeScript SDK enforces (v2.3.1, as shipped in this repo)

The server-side validator (`@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.1,
`dist/mcp-*.mjs`, `validateToolOutput`) makes the outputSchema obligation concrete:

- A tool with an `outputSchema` whose result has no `structuredContent` is **rejected**:
  `Output validation error: Tool <name> has an output schema but no structured content was
  provided` (JSON-RPC `InvalidParams`). Text-only results are not allowed for schema'd tools.
- `structuredContent` is then validated against the schema; a mismatch is rejected the same way.
- The v2 codec's SEP-2106 §4.3 auto-append (so named in the installed SDK's own source;
  implemented as `appendTextFallbackForNonObject`) adds a
  `JSON.stringify(structuredContent)` TextContent block **only when `structuredContent` is a
  non-object** (primitive/array/null) and no text block exists. Object-shaped
  `structuredContent` gets **no** automatic text mirror — the server must mirror it itself to
  satisfy the spec's SHOULD.

Consequence for this repo: the shipped server declares no `outputSchema` and emits both a text
summary and (except for Codex, below) a mirrored `structuredContent` — that combination remains
the spec- and SDK-safe shape. Declaring an `outputSchema` would obligate every successful call
to return schema-conforming structured content.

### Pi 1.3.0: the extension `structuredContent` never reaches the model

From the installed `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` 1.3.0 (the shipped artifact):

- An extension tool's `execute` returns `{ content, structuredContent?, details? }`. The
  `structuredContent` field exists only on the extension **event** layer, documented as
  *"Machine-readable result for tools that declare an `outputSchema`"*
  (`dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts`, `ToolResultEventBase`) — consumers are other extensions
  (hooks, nested tool calls), not the model.
- The model-facing message type (`@earendil-works/pi-ai` `ToolResultMessage`,
  `dist/types.d.ts`) carries `content` blocks, `isError`, ids — no `structuredContent`, and
  `details` is session-record only. The Anthropic serializer sends exactly
  `tool_use_id` + content blocks + `is_error`
  (`dist/api/anthropic-messages.js`, `convertToolResult`).
- So this repo's Pi adapter already does the right thing by putting the full result in the text
  block; its `structuredContent` payload is event-layer data for machine consumers.

### OpenCode 2.0.32: text `content` wins; typed `output` is a JSON-stringified fallback; `metadata` is not model-facing

From the official repo at tag `v2.0.32` (github.com/anomalyco/opencode, where `@opencode/cli`
2.0.32's npm manifest points) and the installed `@opencode/schema`/`@opencode/plugin`:

- `Tool.Result` is `{ output?, content?, metadata? }` — `output` typed by an optional declared
  output schema, `content` a string or text/file blocks, `metadata` a free record
  (`@opencode/schema/dist/tool.d.ts`).
- The model channel is decided by
  [`normalizeContent(content, output)`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.0.32/packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts):
  a string or non-empty `content` wins; only when `content` is absent/empty is `output`
  serialized via `JSON.stringify` into a text block. `metadata` never enters this path (it
  feeds `tool.execute.after` hooks and UI).
- Every tool result then passes through `ToolOutput.truncate`:
  **`MAX_LINES = 2000`, `MAX_BYTES = 50 KiB`** (full output retained to a `tool-output/`
  file for 7 days) — [`packages/core/src/tool-output.ts`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.0.32/packages/core/src/tool-output.ts).
  These caps are also recorded in [control-matrix.md](control-matrix.md#opencode)'s
  OpenCode section.

## What this means for this repo

1. **Text is the only channel verified to reach the model on every host.** Codex is the sole
   host where `structuredContent` demonstrably reaches the model (as a *replacement*); on the
   two native adapters it provably does not (Pi: event-layer only; OpenCode: fallback only).
   Quality fields the model should reason about therefore belong **in the text** — e.g. a
   compact per-result marker like `[rerank 2.1 · authority 3]` (plus `site_name` where present).
   At 10 results that is a few hundred characters, negligible against every cap above.
2. **Mirroring in `structuredContent` stays worth it** for machine consumers (Pi extension
   events, future hosts, tests) and costs nothing: the shipped dual-emission — text plus
   structured, with the mirror omitted for the detected `codex-mcp-client` identity — already
   matches the spec's SHOULD and Codex's replacement. Adding the new fields to both shapes
   changes no host behavior.
3. **Keep `outputSchema` undeclared** on the MCP server unless the team is prepared to guarantee
   schema-conforming `structuredContent` on every successful call (the SDK rejects otherwise).
   The Pi adapter's extension `outputSchema` is safe as-is — Pi re-declares but does not
   validate it, and its `structuredContent` is event data.
4. **New cap facts for the design margin:** OpenCode plugin results truncate at 2000 lines /
   50 KiB, Pi extension tools bypass the MCP 20 KB truncation, Claude Code caps output at
   25k tokens, and Codex applies its per-tool `output_token_limit` (default unpublished).
   None of these bind at search-result volumes; they matter if [inline content](search-inline-content.md) is
   ever enabled.

# Search and fetch API defaults across vendors

This note answers one question: what are the **factory defaults** — the values applied when a
caller passes nothing — of the mature AI-native web-search and web-fetch APIs? It exists
because this repo layers its own client-side defaults on top of the DeepSeek Search/Fetch API,
and the original values (`maxResults=5` on an API `count` of 10, `minRerank=1.5`,
`minAuthority=2`, `allowUnknownAuthority=false`, `maxRetries=0`, `timeout=30s`, fetch
truncation at 16,000 characters, summary truncation at 1,200, response-body cap 5 MiB) were
challenged as arbitrary. The pages below are the benchmark against which the repo's defaults
are grounded; based on this survey the search-side defaults were changed on 2026-10-21 to
`maxResults=10`, `minRerank=0`, `minAuthority=0`, `allowUnknownAuthority=true` (filters stay
available as opt-ins). It records facts only; the closing section lines the repo's values up
against them without recommending changes.

**Research baseline:** 2026-10-21. Claims are cited to primary sources only: official vendor
documentation and official SDK source (GitHub repos and published npm/PyPI packages). Secondhand
blogs and tutorials are excluded. "Default" means the value in force when the parameter is
omitted — not the allowed range, and not an example value. Where no default is published, that
is stated as such rather than guessed.

The five questions asked of every product:

1. Search-result count default (the analogue of this repo's `maxResults`/API `count`).
2. Any **client-side relevance/authority filtering** default (the analogue of
   `minRerank`/`minAuthority`/`allowUnknownAuthority`) — in particular, does anyone drop
   results by authority in the client?
3. HTTP retry default at the SDK layer.
4. Request timeout default (SDK and API layer).
5. Fetched-content truncation default (character limits, byte caps).

# Search with inline content: `need_content` facts

This note answers one question: if DeepSeek's Search API were called with
`need_content: true` (today the repo hardcodes `false`), what would the response provably
contain, what would it cost, how large could it get, and where does that collide with
per-host output caps? It extends
[search-api-defaults.md](search-api-defaults.md) — which surveyed factory defaults — with the
one question that survey did not ask: which vendors ship search-with-inline-content as the
default architecture versus opt-in, and with what per-result content budget. It records facts
only; the closing section lines the facts up against the current two-tool design (search
summary-only plus a separate fetch tool) without recommending for or against it.

**Research baseline: 2026-10-23.** Claims are cited to primary sources only: official
DeepSeek documentation (api-docs.deepseek.com, English and 中文 pages, plus the official FAQ
bundle), other vendors' official documentation and SDK/API references, and OpenAI Codex
source at the repo's locked tag. Secondhand blogs are excluded. Where no primary source pins
a fact — most importantly the size of `content` — that is stated as such: an undocumented
size is itself a decision-relevant fact.

**Short answer:** DeepSeek documents **no size bound** for `need_content` content and no
per-result budget knob; of the eight architectures surveyed below, only Jina ships
content-bearing search as the default; and the binding host cap is Pi's 20 KB MCP-path
truncation — the volume math below puts a safe per-result budget in the ~1k–2k char
range.

## What `need_content=true` provably returns

From the official Search & Fetch guide, the parameter and its response field, verbatim:

| Item | 中文 | English |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `need_content` (request) | “是否在 content 中返回网页正文，为 false 时 content 恒为空字符串。” | "Whether to return page content in content, which is always an empty string when false." |
| `content` (search response) | “网页正文，need_content 为 false 或正文缺失时为空字符串。” | "The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable." |

([指南](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/zh-cn/guides/search) ·
[guide](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/search), checked 2026-10-23.)

Three facts follow, all of them absences:

1. **No size bound of any kind is documented for `content`.** The same guide gives "通常"
   sizing for the other two text fields — `snippet` "通常为 100～200 字符" ("typically 100 to
   200 characters"), `summary` "通常为 600～800 字符" ("typically 600 to 800 characters") —
   but has **no analogous statement** for `content`: no "通常" range, no maximum, no
   truncation rule, no server-side character cap. An undocumented content size is the
   single most decision-relevant fact in this note.
2. **No format statement for search `content`.** The Fetch API's `content` field is
   explicitly Markdown — "The fetched page content as Markdown text." /
   “抓取后的 Markdown 正文” — but the Search API's `content` field carries no format
   statement. Whether search-side `content` is the same Markdown rendering the Fetch
   endpoint returns, or something else, is not documented. “正文缺失时为空字符串”
   ("or when the content is unavailable") implies per-result content can be missing
   independently of `need_content`, which matches the Fetch API's own empty-content failure
   mode; no recovery behavior is specified for search.
3. **No `need_content` × `count` interaction is documented.** The only sentence linking a
   request parameter to result shape is about count and price (below); nothing says content
   is returned for only the top N results, or that `count` behaves differently under
   `need_content`.

## Billing and rate limits

**Billing is per successful request, and `need_content` is never mentioned in connection
with price.** Verbatim from the guide and pricing page:

- “Search 和 Fetch 按请求次数计费，不按 token 或返回结果条数计费” — Search and Fetch are
  billed per request, **not by token or by number of results returned**
  ([指南](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/zh-cn/guides/search)).
- "count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request
  price." / “count 只控制返回的结果条数，不影响单次请求的价格。” (same guide, both languages.)
- Price: Search and Fetch are each "Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75"
  ([pricing](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing); the 中文 pages state
  每 1,000 次成功请求 5 元). A request is billable "only when it returns HTTP 200 and
  produces a result" (Search must return non-empty `results`; Fetch must return page
  content); failures, empty results, and timeouts are free.
- Neither the guide, the pricing page, nor the official FAQ
  (`static.deepseek.com/faq`, whose embedded question set was inspected — it contains zero
  entries about the Search/Fetch API) mentions `need_content` as a price modifier. Under
  the documented model, a `need_content: true` search is one request at the Search
  per-request price; there is no token-metered billing tier for Search/Fetch to move into.

One dated note on the pricing page (verbatim, EN): "when you use the DeepSeek API through
DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex," server-side tool calls already hit the Search and
Fetch APIs; "These calls are currently free of charge;" — “这部分 Search/Fetch 接口调用目前未计费，
并将于北京时间 2026 年 11 月 1 日 00:00 起按次收取调用费用” (per-request billing for those
server-side-tool calls starts 00:00 Beijing time on 2026-11-01 — nine days after this note's

per-request price above, not those chat-completions-internal tool calls.

**Rate limits are per endpoint and independent; `need_content` is not mentioned.** Search
100 QPS, Fetch 25 QPS per account; “Search 和 Fetch 分别独立限速，互不占用额度” ("traffic to
one does not consume the other's quota"); “除了账号级限制，Fetch 还针对目标域名有 QPS 限制”
(Fetch additionally has an unspecified per-domain QPS limit)
([guide](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/search)). A `need_content: true` call is a
Search-endpoint call; no page documents it counting against anything but the Search quota.
